lead: A circular shaft is a long round bar used to carry twisting. When you turn one end while the other is held, every cross-section rotates a little relative to its neighbour. The material resists by shear stress, not by the normal stress of bending. That shear stress is zero on the axis and largest at the outside surface. The torsion formula connects torque, shear stress, radius and a section property called the polar second moment of area, so one equation sizes solid and hollow shafts for pumps, axles, drill pipes and machine tools.
prereq: You need: shear stress and shear modulus from Unit 1, and second moment of area from Unit 4.

blocks.text: Hold one end of a round rubber eraser and twist the other. A straight line drawn along the surface becomes a helix, and a small square on the surface becomes a rhombus. The square has not changed area much; its corners have slid sideways. That sliding is shear strain. A circular shaft works the same way. The twisting moment is torque T, measured in N·m.

Four assumptions make the theory simple. The cross-section is circular and stays circular. A plane cross-section remains plane after twisting and only rotates about the axis. The material is elastic, so Hooke's law applies. Shear stress is proportional to the distance from the centre. The last two assumptions fail after yielding; then the formula gives only an elastic estimate.

Look at a radius in the cross-section. After twist, that radius is still straight, but rotated by angle θ relative to the far end. The shear strain at radius r is γ = rθ/L, where θ is the angle of twist in radians and L is the length in metres. Hooke's law gives τ = Gγ = G r θ/L, with τ the shear stress in Pa and G the shear modulus in Pa. Therefore τ/r = Gθ/L: stress rises in direct proportion to r. At the centre r = 0, so τ = 0. At the outer surface r = R, the stress is largest.

Equilibrium converts the stress pattern into torque. On a small element of area dA at radius r, the force is τ dA and its moment about the axis is τ r dA. Sum over the section: T = ∫ τ r dA. Substitute τ = (Gθ/L) r: T = (Gθ/L) ∫ r² dA. The integral is the polar second moment of area J, in m⁴. So T = GθJ/L.

blocks.where: τ is shear stress at radius r (Pa); r is radial distance from the centre (m); T is torque (N·m); J is polar second moment of area (m⁴); G is shear modulus (Pa); θ is angle of twist over length L (rad); L is length (m).

blocks.text: The same relation gives τ = T r/J. The maximum stress is at r = R: τmax = T R/J. The quantity J/R is the polar section modulus, in m³.

items: Solid shaft of diameter d: J = πd⁴/32.
Hollow shaft, outer diameter D and inner diameter d: J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32.
Use radius, not diameter, in τ = T r/J.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call J the polar moment of inertia and call the result the torsion equation; the symbol and meaning are the same.

A hollow shaft removes material near the axis, where stress is small, and leaves it near the surface, where stress is large. For the same outer diameter and the same torque, a hollow shaft has a smaller J, so its maximum stress is slightly higher. But it also has much less area and mass. That is why drive shafts and axles are often tubes.

Take D = 60 mm outer for both. A solid shaft has J = 1.272 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. A hollow shaft with d = 30 mm has J = (15/16) × 1.272 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.193 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, while its area is 75% of the solid area. At T = 2.5 kN·m, τmax rises from 59.0 MPa to 62.9 MPa, a 6.7% penalty for a 25% mass saving. The trade is usually worth it.

Use the torsion formula for a first size check on a shaft. Then check angle of twist in 6.2. A shaft that is strong enough may still be too flexible, and a lathe spindle or a camshaft can fail a stiffness limit before it fails in stress.

figure.caption: Shear stress against radius for a solid shaft and for a hollow shaft with inner radius half the outer radius. Both lines are straight; the hollow shaft has no material inside r/R = 0.5, so its stress starts at half the maximum.

spec.aria: Line graph: shear stress rises linearly from zero at the centre to maximum at the surface for a solid shaft; for a hollow shaft it starts at half the maximum at the inner radius.

examples.question: A solid steel shaft of diameter 60 mm carries a torque of 2.5 kN·m. Find the maximum shear stress. Take π = 3.1416.
steps: Convert the data: T = 2.5 kN·m = 2500 N·m; d = 60 mm = 0.060 m; R = d/2 = 0.030 m.
Polar second moment: J = πd⁴/32 = π(0.060)⁴/32 = 1.272 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴.
Maximum shear stress: τmax = T R/J = 2500 × 0.030 / (1.272 × 10⁻⁶) = 5.90 × 10⁷ Pa.
examples.answer: The maximum shear stress is 59.0 MPa.

traps: Using diameter d in place of radius r in τ = T r/J. This doubles the stress.
For a hollow shaft, writing D⁴ − d⁴ but subtracting diameters first, as (D − d)⁴. The fourth powers are separate.
Mixing N·m with mm⁴. Use metres throughout, or millimetres throughout, and remember 1 N/mm² = 1 MPa.
Thinking maximum shear stress is at the centre of the shaft. It is zero there and maximum at the outer surface.
Confusing polar second moment J = πd⁴/32 with the second moment about a diameter I = πd⁴/64.

quiz.q: Write the torsion formula and state what each symbol means.
quiz.a: τ/r = T/J = Gθ/L. τ is shear stress at radius r, T is torque, J is polar second moment of area, G is shear modulus, θ is angle of twist and L is length.

quiz.q: Give J for a solid circular shaft of diameter d.
Why is shear stress zero at the centre of a twisted shaft?
quiz.a: Shear strain is γ = rθ/L, so at r = 0 the strain is zero. Hooke's law then gives τ = Gγ = 0.

quiz.q: Why does a hollow shaft use material better than a solid shaft of the same outer diameter?
quiz.a: Stress is largest near the surface. A hollow shaft removes low-stress material near the axis and keeps material where it carries more load, so it saves mass.

quiz.q: A hollow shaft has outer diameter 80 mm and inner diameter 40 mm. Find J.
A solid shaft of diameter 40 mm has maximum shear stress 50 MPa. Find the torque.
For the same torque and same outer diameter, compare τmax in a solid shaft and a hollow shaft with d/D = 0.5.
quiz.a: Jhollow = (1 − 0.5⁴) Jsolid = (15/16) Jsolid. Since τmax = T R/J, τhollow/τsolid = 16/15 = 1.067. The hollow shaft stress is 6.7% higher.

quiz.q: A shaft carries torque only. If its diameter is doubled, what happens to τmax for the same torque?
quiz.a: J ∝ d⁴ and R ∝ d, so τmax = T R/J ∝ d/d⁴ = 1/d³. Doubling d makes τmax one-eighth of its original value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real shafts often carry fluctuating torque and stress concentrations at keyways and shoulders, so fatigue design uses a modified torsion formula. Non-circular shafts need membrane analogy or numerical methods because plane sections do not stay plane. Composite shafts with bonded layers appear in lightweight drives. Search for 'torsion of non-circular bars', 'stress concentration in keyways' and 'fatigue of shafts'.
